analysis_steps.goal: Measure continuum flux density, peak intensity, and core size, and model radial intensity profile

method.value: Fit 2D Gaussian to continuum images at 4 frequencies using IMFIT; construct radial profile at 2.32 mm in 0.1'' concentric annuli and fit 5 analytical models (Single Power-law, Single Plummer, Broken Power-law, Double Plummer, Plummer + Gaussian).

evidence.quote: To estimate the physical parameters of the continuum emission images, we fitted a 2-D Gaussian using the IMFIT task over the main core.
The radial intensity profile was constructed by azimuthally averaging the 2.32 mm continuum emission image in concentric annuli binned at 0.1$^{\prime\prime}$ centered on the emission peak.

The models include (A) a single power-law, (B) a single Plummer-like profile (cite: pl11), (C) a broken power-law, (D) a double Plummer profile, and (E) a Plummer profile with an additional Gaussian component (Plummer + Gaussian).

The fits were performed on the azimuthally averaged radial profile binned at $0.1\ensuremath{''}$ intervals, with the beam profile of $2.30^{\prime\prime} \times 1.28^{\prime\prime}$ ($\sim$ 3791 AU).

findings_qualitative.value: The 2.32 mm radial continuum intensity profile of NIRS3 is best described by a composite Plummer + Gaussian model, indicating a centrally concentrated core with an additional radially localized component.

evidence.quote: The Plummer + Gaussian model (Model E) provides the best fit.

The residuals show minimal systematic deviations across the radial range, with a reduced $\chi^2 = 13.64$, confirming that Model E provides the most robust representation of the observed profile among the five models considered.

findings_qualitative.value: All six detected N-bearing molecules have high excitation temperatures (175-220 K) and compact, spatially unresolved emission (2.20''-2.31'') that arises from the warm inner hot core region (T >= 100 K) of NIRS3.

evidence.quote: The high excitation temperatures (175–220 K) indicate that the identified N-bearing molecules arise from the warm inner regions ($T \geq 100$ K) of the source.

It appeared that the emitting diameters of the different N-bearing molecular transitions are smaller than the synthesized beam sizes of the integrated emission maps, implying that the detected transitions of the N-bearing molecules are spatially unresolved.

findings_qualitative.value: NIRS3 displays unusually high relative abundances of the amide-like molecules NH2CN and NH2CHO compared to other hot cores and hot corinos.

evidence.quote: These results demonstrate that, although the cyanide-bearing species in NIRS3 are not as extreme as in Sgr B2 (N), the source is chemically unique in terms of its exceptionally high relative abundances of and .

claims.hypothesis: The radial continuum intensity distribution of NIRS3 requires a multi-component structural model rather than a single power-law or single Plummer profile.
claims.experiment: Azimuthally averaged the 2.32 mm continuum image in 0.1'' concentric annuli and fitted five analytical models (Single Power-law, Single Plummer, Broken Power-law, Double Plummer, and Plummer + Gaussian), evaluating goodness-of-fit using reduced chi^2 and AIC.
claims.result: Model E (Plummer + Gaussian) achieved the lowest AIC (881.2) and reduced chi^2 (13.64), favored by Delta AIC = 9.3 over Double Plummer and Delta AIC > 25 over single-component models.
claims.finding: A single power-law is insufficient; the radial profile is best represented by a centrally concentrated Plummer-like core plus an additional Gaussian component.

evidence.quote: The Plummer + Gaussian model (Model E) provides the best fit.
It is favored by $\Delta\mathrm{AIC} = 9.3$ relative to the next best model (Double Plummer), while the remaining models show $\Delta\mathrm{AIC} > 10$, indicating little or no empirical support.

claims.hypothesis: Complex N-bearing molecules in S255IR NIRS3 originate from the warm inner hot molecular core region (T >= 100 K).
claims.experiment: Extracted spectra from a 2.32'' circular region in ALMA Band 4 cubes and performed LTE MCMC spectral fitting in CASSIS alongside moment-0 2D Gaussian spatial fitting.
claims.result: Derived excitation temperatures between 176 K and 220 K for all six N-bearing species, with compact emitting region diameters between 2.20'' and 2.31'' centered on the dust continuum peak.
claims.finding: The high excitation temperatures (175-220 K) and compact spatial distributions confirm that the detected N-bearing species emit from the warm inner hot core region of NIRS3.

evidence.quote: The column densities and excitation temperatures of these molecules were derived through LTE spectral modelling, yielding excitation temperatures in the range of 175–220 K. The high excitation temperatures (175–220 K) indicate that the identified N-bearing molecules arise from the warm inner regions ($T \geq 100$ K) of the source.
We find that the integrated emission maps of all detected transitions of N-bearing molecules are very compact towards dust continuum emissions.

claims.hypothesis: Cyanide-family molecules (CH3CN, C2H3CN, and C2H5CN) are chemically linked across star-forming regions.
claims.experiment: Constructed a Pearson correlation coefficient heat map comparing abundances relative to CH3OH and excitation temperatures across NIRS3 and 8 other hot cores and hot corinos.
claims.result: Found strong positive abundance correlations (r >= 0.7) among CH3CN, C2H3CN, and C2H5CN, as well as a strong correlation between the excitation temperatures of C2H5CN and C2H3CN.
claims.finding: The strong positive correlations indicate that CH3CN, C2H3CN, and C2H5CN are chemically linked.

evidence.quote: A Pearson correlation heat map of the abundances reveals a strong positive correlation ($r > 0.7$) among three molecules in the cyanide family, such as , , and , suggesting that these N-bearing molecules may be chemically linked.
There is a strong correlation ($r \geq 0.7$) between all three molecules in the cyanide family, , , and , indicating that there might be potential chemical connections between these molecules.

claims.hypothesis: The observed gas-phase abundances of N-bearing molecules in NIRS3 can be explained by grain-surface formation pathways in three-phase warm-up astrochemical models.
claims.experiment: Compared observed fractional abundances relative to H2, CH3OH, and CH3CN with predictions from published three-phase warm-up chemical models.
claims.result: Observed abundances relative to H2 agree with specific model predictions within factors of 1.04 (CH3CN), 0.67 (C2H5CN), 1.28 (C2H3CN), 0.76 (NH2CN), 0.72 (NH2CHO), and 0.96 (HC3N v7=2), though abundances relative to CH3OH and CH3CN often diverge from Models A and B.
claims.finding: The agreement of H2-normalized abundances with warm-up models supports grain-surface hydrogenation and radical-addition formation pathways, although tailored chemical modelling is needed to confirm the dominant pathways.

evidence.quote: Comparison with three-phase warm-up chemical models shows that the observed abundances of , , , , , and ($\nu_{7}$ = 2) relative to are consistent with model predictions within factors of 1.04, 0.67, 1.28, 0.76, 0.72, and 0.96, respectively.
However, a more detailed analysis of dominant chemical pathways in tailored chemical models is required to confirm these proposed interpretations.

why_this_data.value: NIRS3 hosts a chemically rich hot molecular core where O- and S-bearing species were previously studied, but complex N-bearing species had received little emphasis; archival ALMA Band 4 DDT observations provided sufficient spectral coverage to detect multiple N-bearing transitions.

evidence.quote: Previous studies by (cite: zin15) and (cite: liu20) identified rotational emission lines of numerous oxygen (O)- and sulphur (S)-bearing molecules toward NIRS3, but placed little emphasis on complex N-bearing species.
However, the available spectral coverage enables the detection of several molecular transitions, which we exploit here to investigate the chemical properties of the source.

why_this_method.value: LTE spectral modelling with CASSIS is justified because the inner gas density of NIRS3 (~3x10^7 cm^-3) is comparable to or exceeds the critical density of dense gas tracers (~10^7 cm^-3), thermalizing energy levels; AIC is used to balance goodness of fit against model complexity for radial profiles.

evidence.quote: The AIC balances the goodness of fit against model complexity and is defined as:

The assumption of LTE is valid in the inner region of NIRS3, where the gas density is approximately 3$\times$10$^{7}$ cm$^{-3}$ (cite: sz18), comparable to the critical density of dense gas tracers such as C$^{34}$S($J$ = 7-6) ($\sim10^{7}$ cm$^{-3}$) (see (cite: zin20)).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Four alternative radial intensity profile models (Single Power-law, Single Plummer, Broken Power-law, Double Plummer) were fitted and rejected in favor of the Plummer + Gaussian model based on higher reduced chi^2 and Delta AIC >= 9.3.

evidence.quote: The single power-law fit (Model A) gives $\alpha = 2.20 \pm 0.06$, but this model provides the poorest fit (reduced $\chi^2 = 20.23$) and is strongly disfavored by the model selection criteria, confirming that a single power-law is insufficient to describe the complex structure.

Model E is statistically preferred over the other four models. It is favored by $\Delta\mathrm{AIC} = 9.3$ relative to the next best model (Double Plummer), while the remaining models show $\Delta\mathrm{AIC} > 10$, indicating little or no empirical support.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Direct grain-surface reaction CH3 + CN -> CH3CN (Reaction 1) and HC2N + H -> HC3N (Reaction 3) were rejected as primary formation pathways due to ice interaction barriers, competing reactions with H2O ice, and unverified/assumed rate constants.

evidence.quote: Therefore, there is a low probability of the formation of using reaction 1 on the grain surface of the hot cores.
We also noticed that the rate constants of reaction 3 are assumed. So, we are reluctant to use reaction 3 as the probable formation chain for .

limitations_admitted.value: Short on-source integration time (5.04 minutes) and observations not originally optimized for astrochemistry.

evidence.quote: The on-source integration time was 5.04 minutes, which is relatively short, and the observations were not originally optimized for a detailed astrochemical study.

limitations_admitted.value: Even the best-fitting radial profile model has reduced chi^2 > 1 (13.64), and because the source is only marginally resolved compared to the synthesized beam (~2.30'' x 1.28''), derived power-law slopes may be influenced by beam convolution effects.

evidence.quote: However, it is worth noting that even the best-fitting model has reduced $\chi^2 > 1$, suggesting either that the uncertainties may be slightly underestimated or that there is additional small-scale structure not captured by any of these analytical models.

Therefore, while the profile steepening beyond $\sim$1.5$''$–2.0$''$ suggests a change in the physical regime, likely marking the transition from the inner envelope/disk region to the outer envelope, the derived power-law slopes should be interpreted with some caution, as they may still be influenced by beam convolution effects.

limitations_admitted.value: Excitation temperatures of NH2CHO (only two low-energy transitions detected) and HC3N v7=2 (only one rotational J quantum number detected) cannot be robustly constrained without broader spectral coverage.

evidence.quote: The detected two low-energy transitions of cannot robustly constrain the proper excitation temperature.

Since we have detected only one rotational quantum number ($J$) of ($\nu_{7}$ = 2) alongside various vibrational angular momentum quantum numbers ($l$), those lines can not reliably constrain the appropriate excitation temperature.

limitations_admitted.value: Molecular emissions are spatially unresolved, preventing determination of the internal temperature distribution or a quantitative size-temperature relation.

evidence.quote: It appeared that the emitting diameters of the different N-bearing molecular transitions are smaller than the synthesized beam sizes of the integrated emission maps, implying that the detected transitions of the N-bearing molecules are spatially unresolved.
However, owing to the limited parameter space and small sample size in our dataset, we refrain from performing a quantitative analysis.

limitations_admitted.value: Pearson correlation analysis is based on a small sample of only 9 sources, limiting statistical significance.

evidence.quote: However, their study is based on a substantially larger sample ($>$50 sources), whereas our analysis includes only 9 sources. As the statistical robustness of a correlation depends sensitively on the number of data points, the same threshold does not correspond to an equivalent level of significance in the two studies.

referee_caveats_inferred: Radial profile models (Equations 1-5) are fitted directly to the image-plane azimuthally averaged intensity profile without deconvolving or forward-convolving with the elongated synthesized beam (2.30'' x 1.28''), so the fitted core radii (~2.3''-2.6'') primarily reflect the beam shape rather than intrinsic source structure.

Observation was taken during an accretion burst monitoring campaign to track free-free continuum emission, yet the continuum at ~128-142 GHz is treated as purely thermal dust emission when deriving H2 column density and dust mass without subtracting any free-free contribution.

Comparing vibrational state HC3N (v7 = 2, E_up ~ 690 K) column density directly with total gas-phase HC3N abundances in chemical models without accounting for vibrational partition/excitation correction may bias the abundance comparison.

Equation 13 for deconvolved emitting size theta_s = sqrt(theta_50^2 - theta_beam^2) is incompatible with Table 3 where reported emitting region sizes (2.20''-2.31'') are larger than the geometric mean beam (~1.7'') yet stated in the text to be smaller than the synthesized beam.
